title: Number Line Jumps
directAnswer: Two kangaroos start at positions x1 and x2 and jump v1 and v2 units per jump. They land together after some whole number of jumps n if x1 + n·v1 = x2 + n·v2. Rearranged, n = (x1 − x2) / (v2 − v1). The answer is YES when v1 ≠ v2, the division is exact (no remainder), and the quotient n is non-negative. It is O(1) — one divisibility check, no simulation.

remember.pattern: Set positions equal, solve for the jump count
remember.formula:
if v1 == v2: return x1 == x2
if (x1 - x2) % (v2 - v1) == 0 and (x1 - x2) // (v2 - v1) >= 0:
    return "YES"
return "NO"
rules: Both kangaroos take the **same number of jumps** n. Meeting means `x1 + n·v1 == x2 + n·v2`, which solves to `n = (x1 − x2) / (v2 − v1)`.
**Equal speeds (v1 == v2)** can only meet if they already start together — otherwise the gap never changes. Handle this before dividing to avoid divide-by-zero.
The jump count must be a **non-negative integer**: the remainder must be 0 **and** the quotient must be ≥ 0. Skipping the sign check accepts meetings 'in the past'.
The slower-moving kangaroo can never catch the faster one **if it started behind** — the sign check encodes exactly that.
Do **not** simulate jumps in an unbounded loop without a stop condition — if they never meet, a naive `while` runs forever.
whenToUse: Two linear motions and you ask whether they ever coincide
Anything of the form a + n·p == b + n·q for integer n ≥ 0
A 'do they ever collide / sync up' question over discrete steps
A closed-form divisibility test replaces an unbounded simulation
antiSignals: Motion is non-linear (acceleration, varying step) → no clean formula
You must report when they meet repeatedly, not just whether → model cycles
More than two movers with pairwise constraints → CRT / LCM territory
Positions are real-valued, not integers → divisibility no longer applies
remember.takeaway: Whenever two things move at constant speed, 'do they ever meet?' becomes one equation: set the positions equal and solve for the step count. Number Line Jumps reduces to checking that (x1 − x2) is a non-negative multiple of (v2 − v1) — O(1), no loop.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you can turn two linear motions into a single equation, solve for the integer jump count, and guard the divide-by-zero (equal speeds) and the negative-quotient (meeting in the past) cases instead of looping blindly.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Simulating jumps in a loop with no stop condition so the program never terminates when they never meet, or dividing without checking v1 == v2 first and crashing on divide-by-zero.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Write the meeting equation x1 + n·v1 = x2 + n·v2 on the board, solve for n, and call out both guards — equal speeds and non-negative n — before you touch code.

problemStatement:
Two kangaroos are on a number line at positions `x1` and `x2`. The first kangaroo moves `v1` units per jump; the second moves `v2` units per jump. Both jump at the same time, the same number of times.

Return `"YES"` if there is some number of jumps after which both kangaroos are at the **same location**, otherwise return `"NO"`.

Assume the first kangaroo starts at or behind the second (`x1 < x2`).
constraints: The number of jumps must be a whole, non-negative number
understanding: After n jumps the kangaroos sit at x1 + n·v1 and x2 + n·v2. They meet when those two expressions are equal for some non-negative integer n. Because the first kangaroo starts behind, it can only catch up if it jumps farther each time (v1 > v2), and even then only if the starting gap divides evenly by the per-jump gain.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do both kangaroos always make the same number of jumps?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. They jump simultaneously, so we look for a single n that puts both at the same position at the same time.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What if the two speeds are equal?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Then the gap between them never changes. They meet only if they already start at the same spot — and here x1 < x2, so equal speeds mean NO.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can the meeting happen at a fractional jump?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No. n must be a whole number. If (x1 − x2) is not an exact multiple of (v2 − v1), they pass each other without landing together.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Why does the sign of the quotient matter?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: A negative n would mean they coincided 'before' jumping. Only n ≥ 0 counts, so the quotient must be non-negative.

examples.explanation: Per jump the first gains 1 unit on the second. The 4-unit gap closes after 4 jumps: 0+12 = 12 and 4+8 = 12.
The first kangaroo is both behind and slower, so the gap only grows. They never meet.
The first kangaroo gains 2 units per jump on a starting gap of 84. Since 84 / 2 = 42 is a whole number, they meet after 42 jumps.

approaches.name: Simulation — Jump Until They Meet or Diverge
approaches.whenToMention: Mention as the intuitive model, but stress that it needs a careful stop condition or it loops forever.
hints: Model it literally: advance both kangaroos by their speeds each jump and check whether their positions are equal.
The danger is termination. If the back kangaroo is not faster, the gap never shrinks — your loop must detect that and stop.
Since x1 < x2, stop the moment the first kangaroo reaches or passes the second; if positions matched on the way, the answer is YES, otherwise NO.
approaches.complexityReasoning: The first kangaroo can only catch up if v1 > v2, and then it closes the gap by (v1 − v2) per jump, so the loop runs about (x2 − x1)/(v1 − v2) times — linear in the starting gap. Constant extra space.
approaches.explanation:
This is the version you would animate: nudge both kangaroos forward one jump at a time and watch for a collision.

**Why a naive loop is dangerous.** The obvious code is `while (x1 != x2) { x1 += v1; x2 += v2; }`. If the kangaroos never meet — say the back one is slower — this loop never exits. Any simulation here must carry an explicit termination condition, which is exactly the subtlety the interviewer is probing.

**A correct stop condition.** The first kangaroo starts behind (`x1 < x2`). If it is not strictly faster (`v1 <= v2`) the gap can never shrink, so we answer immediately: YES only if they already coincide, otherwise NO. When `v1 > v2`, the gap shrinks every jump, so we advance until the first kangaroo is no longer behind; if it landed exactly on the second at some point, that final position will be equal.

**Why it is still inferior.** Even with a correct guard, the loop runs proportionally to the starting gap divided by the speed difference — up to ~10⁴ iterations under the constraints. The relationship it is discovering, 'is the gap a multiple of the speed difference?', is a single modulo. Mention the simulation to show you understand the motion, then replace it with the formula.
approaches.insight: A motion simulation that asks 'do they ever meet?' must always answer 'when do I give up?' first. Recognising that the loop closes the gap by a fixed (v1 − v2) per step is the bridge to the closed-form divisibility test.

dryRun.intro: First kangaroo is behind but faster, so the 4-unit gap shrinks by 1 each jump.

code.python:
def kangaroo(x1: int, v1: int, x2: int, v2: int) -> str:
    if v1 <= v2:                  # back kangaroo can never catch up
        return "YES" if x1 == x2 else "NO"
    while x1 < x2:                # close the gap one jump at a time
        x1 += v1
        x2 += v2
    return "YES" if x1 == x2 else "NO"

java.explanation: If the behind kangaroo is not faster, the gap never shrinks — answer now to avoid an infinite loop.
Advance while the first is still behind; this terminates because the gap shrinks each jump.
If the first landed exactly on the second they are equal; if it overshot, they never coincided.

python.explanation: Equal or slower back kangaroo means the gap can only grow or stay — decide immediately.
Loop terminates because v1 > v2 guarantees the gap decreases each jump.
Exact landing is YES; overshoot is NO.

pitfalls: Writing `while (x1 != x2)` with no guard — loops forever when they never meet.
Forgetting the v1 <= v2 early exit, the only thing keeping the loop bounded.
Assuming the first kangaroo is always behind without checking — true here by constraint, but state it.

approaches.name: Divisibility Formula — Solve for n (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want. Derive n from the meeting equation and check it is a non-negative integer.
hints: Set the positions equal: x1 + n·v1 = x2 + n·v2. Group the n terms and solve for n directly.
You get n = (x1 − x2) / (v2 − v1). They meet at a real jump count n that must be a whole number and non-negative.
Guard v1 == v2 first (that makes the denominator zero). Otherwise it is YES exactly when the division has no remainder and the quotient is ≥ 0.
approaches.complexityReasoning: A subtraction, a modulo, a division and two comparisons — a fixed number of operations independent of the inputs. O(1) time and space.
approaches.explanation:
Solve the meeting condition algebraically instead of stepping through it.

**Deriving n.** Meeting after n jumps means `x1 + n·v1 = x2 + n·v2`. Move the position terms to one side and the n terms to the other: `x1 − x2 = n·v2 − n·v1 = n·(v2 − v1)`. Therefore `n = (x1 − x2) / (v2 − v1)`. That single expression is the entire problem — every check below is just validating that this n is a legal jump count.

**Guard the denominator.** If `v1 == v2` the denominator is zero and the division is undefined. Physically, equal speeds mean the gap never changes, so they meet only if they already start together. Since the problem gives `x1 < x2`, equal speeds always answer NO. Handle this branch before dividing.

**The remainder must be zero.** n has to be a whole number of jumps. If `(x1 − x2) % (v2 − v1) != 0`, the kangaroos cross between jumps and never share a position. The modulo is the exact integrality test.

**The quotient must be non-negative.** Even an exact division can yield a negative n, which would describe a meeting before jumping started — not allowed. Requiring `n >= 0` rejects those. Concretely, when the back kangaroo is slower, the formula produces a negative n and we correctly return NO.

**Putting it together.** YES precisely when `v1 != v2`, the remainder is 0, and the quotient is ≥ 0. No loop, no termination worries.
approaches.insight: One equation replaces the whole simulation: set positions equal, solve for n, then sanity-check that n is a non-negative integer. The two guards — divide-by-zero and negative quotient — map exactly onto the two physical impossibilities: equal speeds, and the slower kangaroo starting behind.

dryRun.intro: Plug into n = (x1 − x2) / (v2 − v1) and validate the quotient.

code.python:
def kangaroo(x1: int, v1: int, x2: int, v2: int) -> str:
    if v1 == v2:                      # denominator would be zero
        return "YES" if x1 == x2 else "NO"
    dx = x1 - x2
    dv = v2 - v1
    meets = dx % dv == 0 and dx // dv >= 0
    return "YES" if meets else "NO"

java.explanation: Equal speeds make v2 − v1 zero; handle it before dividing to avoid a crash.
Numerator of n: the starting gap (negative here because x1 < x2).

java.line: boolean meets = dx % dv == 0 && dx / dv >= 0;
java.explanation: Whole number of jumps (no remainder) AND a non-negative count (no meeting in the past).

python.explanation: Guards divide-by-zero; equal speeds meet only if they start together.

python.line: meets = dx % dv == 0 and dx // dv >= 0
python.explanation: Remainder 0 means integer jumps; quotient ≥ 0 means it happens forward in time.

diagrams.caption: Three gates — non-zero denominator, zero remainder, non-negative quotient.

edgeCases.behavior: v1 == v2 and x1 == x2 → YES at n = 0; they already share a spot.
v1 == v2 but x1 != x2 → NO; equal speeds keep the gap fixed forever.

pitfalls: Dividing before checking v1 == v2 — divide-by-zero crash on equal speeds.
Checking only the remainder and skipping n ≥ 0 — accepts impossible 'past' meetings.
Relying on language-specific modulo sign behaviour; pairing the remainder test with an explicit quotient sign check keeps it portable.

commonMistakes: Looping with `while (x1 != x2)` and no termination guard — infinite loop when they never meet.
Dividing by (v2 − v1) without first handling v1 == v2.
Checking divisibility but forgetting that the jump count must be non-negative.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Unbounded simulation
commonMistakesDetailed.why: If the kangaroos never meet, `while (x1 != x2)` advances forever. A simulation needs an explicit stop condition.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
while x1 != x2:      # never exits when they don't meet
    x1 += v1
    x2 += v2
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
if v1 <= v2:
    return "YES" if x1 == x2 else "NO"
while x1 < x2:       # bounded: gap shrinks each jump
    x1 += v1
    x2 += v2

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Divide-by-zero on equal speeds
commonMistakesDetailed.why: v2 − v1 is zero when speeds match. Dividing without guarding crashes; physically equal speeds keep the gap constant.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad: int n = (x1 - x2) / (v2 - v1);   // crashes when v1 == v2
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
if (v1 == v2) return x1 == x2 ? "YES" : "NO";
int dx = x1 - x2, dv = v2 - v1;

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Forgetting the non-negative quotient
commonMistakesDetailed.why: An exact division can still be negative, describing a meeting before any jump. Only n ≥ 0 is a real answer.
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
int dx = x1 - x2, dv = v2 - v1;
return (dx % dv == 0 && dx / dv >= 0) ? "YES" : "NO";

patternNote: Two linear motions meeting reduces to one equation. Set position(t) equal for both movers and solve for the step count; then verify it is a non-negative integer. The two guards — equal rates (no solution) and negative count (solution in the past) — recur in any collision or synchronisation question.
